name: Shabad Shazam
summary: Recognizing indexed Gurbani recordings from a short audio sample, with hymn and performer details in a mobile interface.
question: How can a short audio recording lead a listener to the corresponding Gurbani hymn and performer?
context: Shabad Shazam is a mobile application prototype for identifying recordings from an indexed catalog of Gurbani, the sacred hymns of the Sikh tradition. The application connects microphone capture to an acoustic-fingerprinting service and presents recording metadata and external listening links.
role: Personal project spanning the Flutter interface, recognition-service integration, audio-fingerprinting pipeline, metadata ingestion, and local backend setup.

work.title: Fingerprinting the recording
work.text: Spectral analysis identifies prominent peaks in the audio. Peak-pair hashing converts those features into compact fingerprints, which are matched against a PostgreSQL catalog using time alignment.

work.title: Connecting recognition to the listener
work.text: A Flutter interface captures microphone audio and sends it to FastAPI services. Results return hymn and performer information, alongside local search history and external listening links.

work.title: Building the catalog workflow
work.text: A CSV-driven ingestion workflow generates fingerprints and maintains recording metadata. Docker Compose provides a reproducible local environment for the backend and database.

outcome: The prototype brings audio capture, catalog matching, and recording information into one application flow.
limits: Recognition is limited to recordings present in the indexed catalog. Identification of arbitrary live performances, store publication, and production-scale accuracy or latency are not established.
takeaway: The catalog and ingestion workflow are as important as the matching algorithm: recognition depends on having the right reference recordings and reliable metadata.

name: Neuro Data Lab
summary: A PyQt toolbox for EEG preparation and movement classification, exploring a foundation for brain-controlled interaction.
question: Can EEG recorded during forward and backward movement visualizations be classified into directional categories?
context: The team investigated EEG-based interaction by collecting recordings while participants viewed movement visualizations in a first-person graphical simulation. Game control motivated the work; the completed scope focused on data collection, preparation, and offline classification.
role: Collaborated with the capstone team on the experimental workflow and development of a PyQt toolbox for EEG preparation, Independent Component Analysis, and classifier evaluation.

work.title: Collecting labeled signals
work.text: Multiple participants wore a 14-channel EEG headset while viewing forward and backward movement visualizations. Timed directional cues supplied labels for the collected data.

work.title: Making analysis accessible
work.text: A PyQt toolbox supported EEG data preparation and Independent Component Analysis, bringing the preparation and modeling stages into a graphical workflow.

work.title: Comparing classification approaches
work.text: Five machine-learning classifiers were trained and evaluated. Extra Trees reached 95.45% accuracy in the project's offline evaluation.

outcome: The project produced a graphical analysis toolbox and an offline classification result that provides a starting point for mapping EEG signals to directional commands.
limits: The reported accuracy describes the project's offline evaluation. It does not establish performance on unseen participants or sessions, and live EEG-driven game control was future scope.
takeaway: Evaluation design determines what a model result can support. Subject- and session-independent testing would be an important next step toward practical interaction.

name: DriveSafe
summary: Webcam-based drowsiness monitoring with timed alerts, alongside an Arduino safety-response simulation.
question: How can sustained signs of driver drowsiness be distinguished from brief eye and mouth movements?
context: DriveSafe combines a real-time webcam-monitoring prototype with a separately tested vehicle-control simulation. The vision component looks for prolonged eye closure, yawning, and indicators of distraction; the simulation explores obstacle-aware motor responses.
role: Contributed across detection, sensing, motor-control simulation, testing, integration, and documentation as part of a capstone team.

work.title: Measuring facial movement
work.text: OpenCV handles video capture and image preprocessing, while dlib supplies 68-point facial landmarks. Separate normalized eye-opening and mouth-opening measurements support drowsiness detection.

work.title: Responding to sustained patterns
work.text: Time-based detection logic distinguishes sustained signs of drowsiness from short facial movements. Visual and audible warnings escalate when the detected condition persists.

work.title: Simulating a safety response
work.text: An Arduino-based control system was developed and tested in Tinkercad using four ultrasonic sensors, motor control, and staged deceleration to explore obstacle-aware responses.

outcome: The team developed a driver-monitoring prototype with escalating alerts and a simulated obstacle-aware motor-control workflow.
limits: The vehicle-control component was simulated in Tinkercad. Road deployment and a demonstrated automated connection between the vision detector and control simulation are outside the established scope.
takeaway: Timing and state transitions matter alongside detection: a warning system must account for brief movements, sustained conditions, and recovery.

name: MED-e-CARE
summary: A pharmacy-management application connecting customer ordering, inventory administration, and an NGO ordering workflow.
question: How can customer ordering, pharmacy inventory, and NGO medicine availability be represented in one application?
context: MED-e-CARE was developed as an end-to-end academic pharmacy-management web application during the COVID-19 pandemic. An HTML interface connected to Python backend logic and a relational database.
role: Co-developed customer and administrative workflows, the NGO ordering flow, and the supporting requirements and relational-data design.

work.title: Supporting the customer journey
work.text: The application covered registration, login, account management, medicine selection, order placement, and order history.

work.title: Managing pharmacy operations
work.text: Administrative functions supported inventory updates and sales tracking. Customer, stock, and order information were represented in a SQL database.

work.title: Modeling a distinct ordering workflow
work.text: An NGO ordering flow used expiry-based medicine availability. UML models translated application requirements into relationships and interactions among users, inventory, and orders.

outcome: The project brought customer ordering, inventory administration, and NGO availability into a connected application with an explicit relational model.
limits: This was an academic application. Production adoption, payment-gateway integration, and operational usage metrics are not established.
takeaway: Clear requirements and a coherent data model make it easier to connect different user roles without treating each workflow as a separate application.
